definition: One of the periods a school year is divided into.
example: The school term ends in June.
note: Spanish gave a vague 'period' and German 'Semester' is used for universities, not schools. All four now say the same thing.

definition: The rails a train runs along.
example: The train runs on the track.
note: Italian was plural while the other three were singular. Made singular.

example: I am having trouble understanding this new lesson.
note: Italian 'guaio' means being in a scrape or a mess, which is stronger than the definition. Changed to 'difficoltà'.

definition: A place where an event is held.
example: The band played at a new venue in the city centre.
note: Italian 'locale' means a bar or club rather than any event place. Changed to 'sede'.

example: This is a good way to learn new vocabulary.
note: Same word appears twice in the list with different German. Set to 'Art' so the two entries agree.

definition: Used to refer to the person receiving an action.
example: To whom did you give the book?
note: French was missing the little linking word that Spanish and Italian both have. Added.

example: She has not finished her homework yet.
note: French 'pas encore' already contained the word 'not'. Removed so it matches the other three.

definition: To use up all of something.
example: We will run out of milk soon.
note: Italian 'esaurire' is what you do to a supply, not what happens to you. Changed to 'restare senza', matching the Spanish.

example: Please come in and sit down.
note: Italian 'accomodarsi' means 'take a seat', not 'come in'. Changed to 'entrare'.

definition: To be found or appear unexpectedly.
example: My lost keys finally turned up in the sofa cushions.
note: French 'réapparaître' means 'to appear again'. Changed to 'apparaître' so all four match.

example: Her eyes started tearing up during the sad film.
note: French 'en larmes' described a state rather than the action. Changed to a phrase that means the eyes are filling with tears.

example: The old car broke down on the way home.
note: Spanish 'romperse' just means 'to break'. The word for a vehicle or machine failing is 'averiarse'.

definition: To invent a story or excuse.
example: He had to make up a reason for being late.
note: German was missing the small reflexive word it needs. Added.

definition: To see or hear something with difficulty.
example: I can barely make out the words on this old sign.
note: Spanish and Italian said 'to understand', which is a different idea. Both changed to 'to make out with difficulty', matching the definition.

definition: To move at the same speed as someone else.
example: She walks quickly, so I must walk fast to keep up.
note: French 'continuez' was a command form ('carry on'), which is not what the word means here. Spanish 'mantenerse' was too vague. Both changed to match the definition.
